analysis.one_liner: Raises estate and gift taxes on multimillion-dollar inheritances and closes trust loopholes.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2023 with 3 sponsors, never received a committee vote or floor vote in the Senate, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the estate tax on very large inheritances: it cuts the amount any estate can pass on tax-free to $3.5 million, adds new rates rising to 65% on the portion of an estate above $1 billion, and closes common techniques that wealthy families use to shield assets from tax, including certain trusts and valuation discounts. It also raises protections for family farms and land donated for conservation. In practice, it would affect only the largest estates — hence the name 'For the 99.5 Percent.'
analysis.who_benefits: Families with no expectation of leaving a multimillion-dollar estate — effectively all but the wealthiest 0.5% of households. The bill imposes no new tax on them, while the added revenue from the largest estates could reduce the deficit or fund public programs. The bill also widens special tax breaks for family farms and for land put under conservation easements.

how_it_helps.text: The bill leaves estates valued at $3.5 million or below entirely unaffected, meaning roughly 99.5% of households pay no new tax.
It adds a new 65% rate on the portion of an estate above $1 billion, meaning the largest dynastic fortunes pay the most.
It raises the special farmland valuation reduction from $750,000 to $3 million, indexed for inflation, making it easier for farm families to keep land in the family.
It raises the estate-tax exclusion for land donated under conservation easements from $500,000 to $2 million and increases the applicable percentage to 60%, encouraging land conservation.
It requires disclosure to Treasury and to recipients of the value of each interest in an estate or gift, closing information gaps that currently make enforcement difficult.

analysis.who_pays: Estates and gifts above $3.5 million, and especially the wealthiest families whose estates exceed $1 billion. Families that use sophisticated estate-planning structures — grantor trusts, short-term GRATs, and valuation discounts — to pass wealth with minimal tax would also face higher taxes. Estate-planning professionals who sell those techniques would lose business.

drawbacks.text: Cutting the tax-free exclusion from roughly $13 million to $3.5 million per person affects far more than billionaires: a couple passing on a $7 million estate, which can include a house, retirement accounts, and a small business in a high-cost region, would face the tax for the first time.

The changes to trusts, valuation discounts, and gift exclusions are technically complex and would require significant new compliance work from executors, families, and the Treasury, and could prompt years of litigation over valuation.
Opponents of estate taxation argue that taxing inherited wealth can force asset sales, though the bill specifically raises the farmland valuation break to $3 million to blunt that effect on farms.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the overwhelming majority of households the bill has no cost — it simply does not apply to them. The real tradeoff falls on wealthy families and their advisors: a substantially higher tax on very large inheritances in exchange for closing avoidance techniques, while the bill deliberately sweetens protections for farms and conservation land. The main honest criticism is the lower $3.5 million threshold, which reaches upper-middle-wealth estates in expensive regions, not just the ultra-rich the bill's name targets.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced the bill and the Senate sent it straight to the Finance Committee, which never voted on it, so it died quietly when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sanders introduced the bill with Warren on April 18, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
Two additional Senate Democrats signed on as cosponsors.
No further action appears in the record: the Finance Committee never held a markup, the bill never reached the Senate floor, and it expired at the end of the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households with estates large enough to be affected, and the trust-and-estate planning industry that serves them, since current tax rates, exemption levels, and avoidance techniques remain intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large estates and their planning advisors

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and named it the 'For the 99.5 Percent Act.'

for.name: Elizabeth Warren
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; original cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders in introducing the bill at its introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred under Chairman Ron Wyden
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no markup, no vote — leaving it to expire without reaching the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the chamber's true split is unknown; support shown in the record came only from one Independent and three Democrats, with no Republicans or other Democrats recorded either way.

industries.industry: Ultra-wealthy households with estates over $3.5 million
industries.note: The bill would tax the portion of estates above $3.5 million at rates up to 45%, and up to 65% above $1 billion. Avoiding these taxes by sheltering large inheritances means the tax burden stays on everyone else or public revenue shrinks.

The bill curtails the main techniques the industry sells to shrink taxable estates: short-term GRATs, grantor trusts, valuation discounts for family-controlled entities, and dynasty trusts that skip generations. Their gain from blocking the bill comes at the cost of tax enforcement and revenue.

industries.industry: Family farms and small working-land owners
industries.note: The bill quadruples the special farmland valuation reduction to $3 million and expands the conservation-easement exclusion to $2 million at a 60% rate, making it easier to pass farm and forest land to the next generation. Some farms in high-value regions could still face the lower overall exclusion.

industries.industry: Land trusts and conservation easement donors
industries.note: A larger estate-tax exclusion and higher percentage for donated conservation easements would strengthen the incentive to place land under permanent conservation.
